title: Kris Jenner Reveals Why Her Late Ex-Husband Robert Kardashian Had 'Unrestricted Access' to Her Home Years After Their Divorce
excerpt: Kris Jenner opens up about the co-parenting philosophy she built with Robert Kardashian after their 1991 split — and why she still stands by it decades later.
body: Kris Jenner has spent decades in the public eye as the architect of one of the most famous families in America, but in a recent conversation on Jay Shetty's podcast On Purpose, she pulled back the curtain on something far more personal than business strategy: how she managed to stay close, even domestically close, with the man she divorced more than three decades ago.

The revelation centers on her first husband, attorney Robert Kardashian, who Kris says had what she described as an open invitation to walk into her home whenever he wanted, long after their marriage had legally ended. She told Shetty that Robert knew he could come through the back door at any hour, and that he could count on dinner being ready at 6 p.m. There was no need to call ahead, no need to check if it was a good time. He was, in her words, simply always welcome.

That kind of arrangement is unusual by most divorce standards, where boundaries are drawn and former spouses often become polite strangers at best. But Kris explained that this level of comfort didn't happen overnight. She was candid about the fact that it took her a couple of years after the divorce to get to a place where she could extend that kind of unguarded welcome to Robert. Healing, she suggested, isn't instant, even when both parties want to move forward peacefully for the sake of their children.

Kris and Robert Kardashian married in 1978 and divorced in 1991, a split that came before Kris's marriage to Caitlyn Jenner, then known as Bruce Jenner. Robert and Kris had four children together: Kourtney, Kim, Khloé, and Rob Kardashian. Long before the family became a reality television phenomenon with Keeping Up with the Kardashians, Robert was already a fixture in the American cultural consciousness for a very different reason — his role as part of O.J. Simpson's defense team during the 1995 murder trial that captivated the nation.

What makes Kris's recent comments notable is how deliberately she framed the choice to keep Robert close as a parenting strategy rather than simply a personal preference. She explained on the podcast that she made a conscious decision early on not to speak badly about her exes in front of her children. In her view, that kind of ongoing criticism does real psychological and emotional damage to kids, who are already processing their own grief over their parents' separation, even when the adults involved have moved on.

That framing — divorce as a form of grief for children, regardless of how amicable the adults manage to be — is one Kris returned to more than once in the conversation. She pointed out that the fathers of her children are, by definition, also the fathers of her grandchildren, and that her feelings toward them didn't simply switch off because the romantic relationship had ended. Loyalty to family, in her telling, extends well past the terms of a marriage license.

According to Kris, that philosophy showed up in tangible ways throughout her children's early lives. Robert Kardashian was present for major family milestones long after the divorce, including Kendall and Kylie Jenner's first birthdays, even though those two daughters were from Kris's marriage to Caitlyn Jenner and not biologically his own. The Kardashian-Jenner children reportedly grew up calling him 'Uncle Robert,' a nickname that speaks to how thoroughly he remained woven into the family's day-to-day life rather than becoming a distant, occasional figure.

Kris also made clear that this wasn't a one-time policy she applied only to her own past relationships. She said she's carried the same approach forward with her daughters' exes as well, extending similar warmth and access to men who were once part of the family through relationships with Kourtney, Kim, Khloé, Kendall, and Kylie. Her reasoning, as she explained it, comes down to legacy: she wants her grandchildren to remember their families being treated with respect and warmth, not division.

It's a philosophy that stands in sharp contrast to how a lot of blended and post-divorce families operate, where former partners are often kept at arm's length, especially once new relationships and new households enter the picture. Kris's approach required not just her own emotional work, but buy-in from her children, from Robert, and later from the various partners who came in and out of her daughters' lives. That kind of sustained cooperation across a large, high-profile family is not easy to maintain, and Kris has acknowledged in other interviews over the years that keeping the peace within the family has required real effort, not just good intentions.

Robert Kardashian's story took a difficult turn in the early 2000s. He was diagnosed with esophageal cancer in the summer of 2003, and passed away just two months later, in September 2003, at the age of 59. His death came relatively early in the Kardashian family's rise to mainstream fame — Keeping Up with the Kardashians wouldn't premiere until 2007 — meaning Robert never saw the full scale of the media empire his children would go on to build. Kim Kardashian has spoken publicly in the years since about how much she wishes her father could have witnessed her success, and about the void his absence left in major family moments.

Kris, for her part, went on to marry Caitlyn Jenner later in 1991, the same year her divorce from Robert was finalized. That marriage produced two more daughters, Kendall and Kylie Jenner, expanding the blended family that would eventually become the center of one of the most-watched reality television franchises in history. Kris and Caitlyn's marriage lasted over two decades before their own split, which played out publicly as Caitlyn transitioned and the family adjusted to a new chapter.

Across both of her major relationships, Kris has consistently framed her post-divorce approach the same way: prioritize the children's emotional stability over any residual bitterness between the adults. That's a message she's repeated in various forms over the years, whether discussing Robert Kardashian, Caitlyn Jenner, or the string of relationships her daughters have navigated in the public eye, from Kim's marriages to Kourtney's long on-and-off relationship with Scott Disick, who himself has often been treated as a permanent extension of the family despite never marrying into it.

The Jay Shetty interview arrives at a moment when Kris Jenner, now in her seventies, has increasingly leaned into a role as something of an elder stateswoman on topics like family, resilience, and reinvention, subjects she's uniquely positioned to speak on given the decades she's spent building both a business empire and a sprawling blended family under constant public scrutiny. Her comments about Robert Kardashian's open access to her home aren't just a nostalgic anecdote — they function as a broader statement about the kind of family culture she says she tried to build on purpose, one rooted in forgiveness and continuity rather than resentment.

Whether or not every family could realistically replicate the specific dynamic Kris describes — an ex-husband with unrestricted access to the family home, welcomed at the dinner table for years after divorce — the underlying message she's offering is a more universal one about co-parenting: that former partners can choose to remain part of a shared family story, and that doing so can be a gift to the children caught in the middle of a split they didn't choose.

title: Oprah Winfrey Reveals Her Real Name Was Never Actually 'Oprah' — And Fans Are Stunned by the Birth Certificate Twist
excerpt: Oprah Winfrey opened up on Keke Palmer's podcast about the biblical name on her birth certificate, the childhood mix-up that changed it forever, and when she actually found out.
body: For nearly five decades, the name Oprah has functioned almost like a brand unto itself — a single word instantly recognizable across the globe, tied to daytime television history, a media empire, and a level of cultural influence few public figures ever achieve. Which is exactly why a recent podcast conversation caught so many people off guard: Oprah Winfrey confirmed that 'Oprah' was never actually the name on her birth certificate.

The revelation came during a candid sit-down on Keke Palmer's podcast, Baby, This Is Keke Palmer, an episode that ranged across topics like self-worth, friendship, and personal history before Keke steered the conversation toward a detail from Oprah's early life that, by Oprah's own admission, still surprises people when they hear it for the first time.

According to Oprah, her birth certificate reads O-R-P-A-H, not O-P-R-A-H. The name Orpah is a biblical reference, pulled from the Book of Ruth in the Old Testament. In that story, two daughters-in-law, Ruth and Orpah, are faced with a choice after being widowed: stay loyal to their mother-in-law, Naomi, or return to their own families and former lives. Ruth famously chooses to stay, delivering one of the most quoted lines of loyalty in the Bible, while Orpah turns back toward her old life instead.

Oprah has referenced this bit of biblical trivia before over the years, often with a sense of self-deprecating humor about being named after the character who, narratively speaking, makes the less celebrated choice in the story. During the Keke Palmer conversation, she leaned into that humor again, joking about the irony of carrying the name of the daughter-in-law who essentially decided the road ahead was too long and turned around.

What's important to understand, though, is that the switch from Orpah to Oprah wasn't a branding decision, a stage name, or a deliberate reinvention the way many celebrities adopt more marketable names for their public careers. Oprah has been clear that the change happened organically, and largely by accident, during her early childhood. People simply struggled to pronounce and spell the unfamiliar biblical name correctly, and over time the 'P' and the 'R' got flipped in everyday conversation and paperwork.

Once people around her started calling her Oprah instead of Orpah, the new pronunciation stuck, and it eventually became the name she was known by in virtually every context, from school to her early broadcasting career in Nashville and Baltimore, all the way through to the launch of The Oprah Winfrey Show in 1986. Yet, remarkably, her actual legal name on paper never changed to match the name the world came to know her by.

Perhaps the most surprising detail from the conversation is just how long it took Oprah herself to fully realize the discrepancy. She told Keke Palmer that she didn't become aware that the name everyone called her wasn't technically her legal name until she was around 20 years old — meaning she spent the first two decades of her life without fully registering that a childhood mispronunciation had permanently altered her public identity.

That detail adds an interesting layer to how identity, names, and public persona can diverge from official documentation without most people ever noticing, even the person living it. In Oprah's case, the discrepancy never caused any real-world complications significant enough to become public knowledge until now, likely because 'Oprah' had already become so thoroughly established as her name in practice long before she was famous enough for anyone to scrutinize a birth certificate.

The moment also opened the door for a lighter, parallel revelation from Keke Palmer herself. During the same conversation, Keke pointed out that her own birth name isn't simply 'Keke' either — she was born Lauren Keyana Palmer, with 'Keke' functioning as a nickname derived from her middle name that eventually became her public identity, not unlike what happened with Oprah. Keke added that among close friends and family, she also goes by 'Eeky,' a more intimate nickname layered on top of the public one.

Interestingly, Oprah revealed she already knew about Keke's full birth name before the podcast conversation, having heard it referenced during one of Keke's TED Talks. That small detail underscores something Oprah has built much of her post-talk-show career around: paying close attention to the guests and public figures she engages with, whether through her book club, her interviews, or her broader media ventures under OWN.

The episode didn't stop at names. It also touched on Oprah's decades-long friendship with Gayle King, one of the most enduring relationships in modern media, as well as reflections on the influence of writer and poet Maya Angelou, who was a close mentor to Oprah for years before Angelou's death in 2014. Oprah has often credited Angelou with shaping her understanding of self-worth, resilience, and what it means to know your own value regardless of outside validation — themes that echoed throughout the Keke Palmer conversation as a whole.

For longtime fans, the name reveal is a small but genuinely fascinating footnote in the larger Oprah story — proof that even one of the most examined public figures of the last half-century still has details about her own origin that can catch an audience by surprise. It's also a reminder of how names, once adopted widely enough by the people around us, can quietly become permanent, regardless of what's written on the original paperwork.

The full episode, released on Keke Palmer's podcast on July 21, has continued to circulate widely since airing, with clips of the birth certificate reveal drawing particular attention across social media as fans reacted to learning that one of the most famous single names in the world was, technically, never the correct one to begin with.

title: Cher Ordered to Pay Her Own $1 Million Legal Bill Despite Winning Royalties Battle Against Sonny Bono's Widow Mary Bono
excerpt: Cher won her royalties dispute against Mary Bono over classics like 'I Got You Babe,' but a federal judge just ruled she has to cover more than $1 million in her own legal fees.
body: Cher has come out on top in a years-long legal battle over song royalties tied to her music with the late Sonny Bono, but a new federal ruling means that victory is coming at a steep personal cost — more than $1 million in unreimbursed legal fees that she'll now have to cover entirely on her own.

A federal judge has denied Cher's request to force Mary Bono, the widow of her ex-husband and former musical partner Sonny Bono, to pay back the legal costs Cher racked up while fighting the case. The ruling closes out one chapter of a dispute that has dragged on for years, even as a related appeal keeps the broader legal saga between the two women alive.

To understand how the case got here, it helps to go back to 1978, the year Cher and Sonny Bono finalized their divorce. As part of that settlement, Cher was entitled to 50% of the publishing royalties generated by the songs the duo had written and recorded together during their years as Sonny & Cher, a catalog that includes enduring hits like 'I Got You Babe' and 'The Beat Goes On.' Those songs have remained culturally relevant for decades, generating ongoing royalty income well beyond the original run of Sonny & Cher's popularity in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

Sonny Bono died in a skiing accident in January 1998, and his estate — including his share of the songwriting catalog and the obligations tied to Cher's divorce settlement — passed to his widow, Mary Bono, who later went on to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives representing California, filling the seat her husband had held before his death.

According to Cher's legal team, the royalty payments that had been flowing to her under the terms of the 1978 divorce agreement were cut off in 2021, prompting her to file suit against Mary Bono to enforce the original settlement terms. In response, Mary Bono's side attempted a different legal strategy entirely: invoking a copyright law provision known as a termination right.

That termination right is a real and fairly well-established piece of U.S. copyright law. It allows songwriters, or their heirs, to reclaim control of songs they wrote decades earlier, effectively terminating older publishing agreements and licensing arrangements after a set number of years, even ones that seemed to be locked in permanently at the time they were signed. Mary Bono's team argued this provision could be used to cut off Cher's ongoing share of the royalties tied to the Sonny & Cher catalog.

The court didn't agree. In a ruling issued in May 2024, the judge sided with Cher, finding that the copyright termination provision Mary Bono was relying on simply didn't apply to this situation. The key distinction, according to the court, was that Cher's right to those royalties came from a divorce settlement — a contract matter governed by California family and contract law — rather than from a copyright assignment that could be unwound using a copyright-specific termination mechanism.

That ruling was significant because it preserved not just Cher's back pay, but her right to keep collecting royalties going forward. A final judgment signed in November 2025 formally confirmed the outcome, determining that Cher was owed more than $418,000 in unpaid royalties that had accumulated since payments stopped in 2021, on top of reaffirming her ongoing 50% share of future publishing income from the catalog.

Having won on the substance of the case, Cher's legal team moved to the next phase of the fight: trying to recoup the money spent getting there. They sought to have Mary Bono cover the $1,023,605 in attorney's fees Cher had incurred throughout the litigation, arguing that Mary had unnecessarily dragged out the proceedings and forced Cher to spend far more than should have been required to enforce a decades-old settlement agreement.

Judge John A. Kronstadt rejected that request. His reasoning came down to the same legal distinction that had actually helped Cher win the case in the first place: because the dispute was ultimately rooted in California contract law rather than the federal Copyright Act, the fee-shifting rules that typically allow a prevailing party in a copyright case to recover their legal costs from the losing side simply didn't apply here. In other words, the very argument that protected Cher's royalties — that this was a contract dispute, not a copyright dispute — is also what prevented her from making Mary Bono pay for the fight.

It's a costly irony. Court filings suggest Cher's total legal spend on the matter isn't even fully settled yet, with roughly $10,000 more expected to be tacked onto her existing bill as remaining costs are finalized. All told, Cher will have spent north of $1 million defending a right to royalties that, on paper, she was always contractually entitled to.

The case isn't fully closed, either. Mary Bono is separately appealing the original May 2024 ruling on the royalties dispute itself at the federal appeals court level, meaning the underlying question of whether the termination right could ever apply to a settlement like this one could still be revisited by a higher court. Until that appeal plays out, both women remain tied up in a legal relationship neither seems eager to continue.

Representatives for both Cher and Mary Bono have so far declined to comment publicly on the fee ruling specifically, though the broader dispute has drawn steady coverage from outlets including TMZ, Rolling Stone, Billboard, and People, given the combination of high-profile names and a genuinely unusual legal question about where copyright law ends and family law begins.

For now, the practical outcome is clear even if the full saga isn't over: Cher gets to keep her royalties and her back pay, but she's paying for that peace of mind entirely out of her own pocket — a reminder that even a clear legal win doesn't always come cheap, especially when the losing side has the resources and motivation to keep appealing.

title: Former Love Island Contestant Malin Andersson Says 'Nobody Knows What's Going On' for People in Reality TV
excerpt: Malin Andersson, who appeared on Love Island alongside Sophie Gradon, has accused the show's producers of failing to support Sophie's mental health after she left the villa — claims raised ahead of a new Prime Video documentary revisiting the show's darkest chapter.
body: Warning: this article discusses suicide, which some readers may find distressing.

On 20 June 2018, two years after appearing on the dating series Love Island, former contestant Sophie Gradon died by suicide. It was a loss that shook the show's fanbase and reignited longstanding questions about how much support reality TV contestants actually receive once the cameras stop rolling and the public attention fades.

Now, a former castmate of the Newcastle-born model has come forward with fresh allegations, claiming the show's producers failed to provide Sophie with the mental health support she needed after leaving the villa, despite claims that she had asked for it directly.

Malin Andersson, who appeared alongside Sophie on the second series of Love Island in 2016, features as a guest contributor in the upcoming two-part docu-series The Curse of Love Island, set to premiere on Prime Video this weekend. The documentary promises an unflinching look at the darker side of reality television, including the deaths of several former contestants who once appeared on the show.

Asked to comment on the series ahead of its release, a spokesperson for ITV told press that it would never be appropriate for the broadcaster to comment on specific steps taken in relation to any individual's welfare, citing medical confidentiality. The spokesperson added that where the documentary may present inaccuracies in an account of how someone was looked after, it's difficult for the broadcaster to contest those claims when it cannot discuss specifics, and noted that ITV does not recognise the events described about the aftercare of contributors as presented in the film.

To understand why Sophie Gradon's story continues to resonate years later, it helps to look back at her time on the show. During her season, Sophie struck up a widely followed romance with Welsh fitness enthusiast Tom Powell, who became a firm fan favourite, particularly among female viewers watching at home. One of the more memorable moments of her time in the villa came when Sophie used a 'Miss Love Island' talent-show segment to speak out about the double standards women face around sexuality, after her co-star Zara Holland had been stripped of a beauty title over reports she'd had sex with a fellow Islander.

After Tom was voted off the island, Sophie went on to form a connection with fellow contestant Katie Salmon, becoming part of what's often cited as the show's first same-sex couple — a moment that added another layer of cultural significance to her time on the series. A few weeks before that season's final, Sophie chose to leave the show voluntarily, telling viewers she wanted to reunite with Tom Powell outside the villa.

Although the on-screen romance with Tom was ultimately short-lived, Sophie's profile only grew after the show ended. She became a familiar face on the red carpet circuit and a regular presence in entertainment magazines, living out what looked from the outside like the glamorous, high-visibility lifestyle many reality contestants hope for when they sign up for a dating show.

According to Malin, that public image masked a much harder private reality. She alleges that at some point after the show, Sophie's mental health reached a breaking point, and that Sophie proactively reached out for help. 'I remember Sophie being upset, and we'd speak,' Malin recalled. 'She was trying to get in touch with Love Island, and she was mad that they weren't giving her a response.'

That account is echoed by Sophie's childhood friend Stephen, who also appears in the documentary. He has admitted that he always feared something like this could happen, describing it as every friend's worst fear coming true when he learned what happened to Sophie.

In the summer of 2018, weeks after the fourth series of Love Island had begun airing, Sophie was found dead at her parents' home by her boyfriend and her brother. Northumbria Police treated her death as a likely suicide at the time, and an inquest later ruled that she had taken her own life while under the influence of drugs and alcohol. Police also confirmed that Sophie had been diagnosed with depression and low self-esteem back in 2013, and had been taking medication for social anxiety disorder prior to her death.

Malin has said the loss of her former castmate forced her to reassess her own understanding of fame and struggle. 'I didn't know she was feeling that bad, to want to do that,' she admitted. 'I think Sophie's death really put things into perspective for us. People think you've just been given a green card and you've got a good life. No way. Nobody knows what's going on truly for people in reality TV.'

Stephen has raised similar concerns about the pressures that come with sudden reality TV fame, saying that being part of the industry Sophie found herself in could cause real anxiety and mental health strain, and suggesting that the difficulties she faced might have looked different had she never appeared on the show at all. He has been direct in saying he believes production needs to offer more support to people once they leave.

Malin has also alleged that producers didn't reach out to her personally until after Sophie's death. 'I didn't get any calls,' she claimed. 'When they did call me after Sophie had died to ask if I was okay, I remember feeling a bit of anger, because I knew they hadn't looked after us properly.' Stephen has offered a similar characterisation of the aftercare process, describing contestants as being thrust into the limelight and then, once the show ends, sent home in a taxi with little in the way of structured follow-up support.

ITV has previously said that its duty of care measures for Love Island contestants have evolved significantly since they were first published in 2019, following broader public concern around the wellbeing of participants across the reality TV genre — concern that intensified industry-wide following a string of high-profile deaths connected to other shows during that period.

The broadcaster has pointed to its published welfare protocols, which include psychological support before, during, and after filming, structured training for participants on how to handle media attention and public behaviour, and a social media blackout period while contestants are still living in the villa. ITV has also said these measures are regularly reviewed by independent Chief Medical Officers, with one saying the safeguards continue to evolve in light of experience and advances in best practice, while another framed the ongoing challenge as balancing contestant welfare with preserving the creative spontaneity that makes the format work.

The upcoming documentary doesn't focus solely on Sophie Gradon's story. It also revisits the death of fellow former Islander Mike Thalassitis, who took his own life in March 2019 at the age of 26, a year after Sophie's death. A toxicology report at the time found that Mike had alcohol, cocaine, and antidepressants in his system when he died. Prior reporting has also indicated that Mike had privately struggled with depression in the months leading up to his death, a battle that reportedly went undisclosed to those closest to him, including his own family, until afterward.

The show's former presenter, Caroline Flack, died by suicide in February 2020 at the age of 40. In the weeks before her death, Flack had been arrested and charged with assaulting her partner, Lewis Burton, and had stepped down from her hosting role on Love Island amid the fallout. Her death, much like Sophie's and Mike's, prompted widespread public reckoning with how reality television franchises support the people at the centre of them, both during production and long after a season wraps.

Responding to Malin's claims and the upcoming Prime Video documentary as a whole, an ITV spokesperson offered a statement extending sympathy to the families of both Sophie and Mike, acknowledging that many members of the production team who worked on the show's earlier years are still working on the series today, and that news of Sophie's and Mike's deaths was, and remains, deeply distressing to everyone who knew them. The broadcaster said both are remembered with great affection.

The Curse of Love Island arrives at a moment when reality television as a genre continues to face scrutiny over how contestants are prepared for, and supported through, the intense and often disorienting experience of sudden fame. For families like Sophie Gradon's, and for former castmates like Malin Andersson, the hope expressed publicly has been that documentaries like this one push the conversation forward rather than simply revisiting old grief for entertainment.

If you or someone you know is struggling with thoughts of suicide, support is available. In the UK, Samaritans can be reached free, any time, on 116 123. In the US, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is available 24/7 by calling or texting 988.

title: Sharon and Kelly Osbourne Pay Emotional Tribute to Ozzy Osbourne on First Anniversary of His Death
excerpt: One year after losing Ozzy Osbourne, Sharon and Kelly Osbourne are opening up about grief, memory, and the moments that still bring him back to life.
body: A year has now passed since the world lost Ozzy Osbourne, and the anniversary has brought his family back into the spotlight — not for a new tour or television project, but to talk openly about grief, memory, and what they miss most about the man behind the legend.

Sharon Osbourne, 73, marked the milestone with an interview on BBC Radio WM, the same station tied to the couple's Birmingham roots, while Ozzy's daughter Kelly Osbourne chose a different medium entirely, posting a long, deeply personal tribute to her father on Instagram on the anniversary itself.

Speaking to the BBC, Sharon focused less on Ozzy's decades of rock stardom and more on the qualities she wants people to remember him for on a human level: his humor, and his refusal to ever be anyone other than exactly who he was. She recalled one of his own jokes about how he'd want to be remembered — by blasting music as loud as physically possible and headbanging along to it, a fittingly irreverent send-off for a man whose entire career was built on turning volume and chaos into art.

Sharon went further, describing Ozzy as someone who never pretended, never performed a version of himself for other people's comfort, and always told the truth even when it wasn't convenient. That honesty, she said, meant she always knew exactly where she stood with him, something she clearly considers rare and valuable after nearly four decades of marriage that included very public highs and very public struggles. Even their worst arguments, she noted, tended to end in laughter, simply because of how absurd Ozzy could be in the middle of a fight.

That kind of memory — imperfect, funny, human — feels consistent with how the Osbourne family has always presented itself publicly, going back to the early 2000s when The Osbournes turned their chaotic, foul-mouthed, deeply loving household into one of MTV's biggest reality shows. Sharon and Ozzy's willingness to be unfiltered on camera decades ago is part of why so much of the public feels like they knew Ozzy personally, not just as a musician but as a specific, recognizable personality.

Kelly Osbourne, 41, took a different approach to the anniversary, choosing the more private, unfiltered space of a long Instagram post rather than a broadcast interview. In it, she described something that grief counselors often talk about but that's rarely put into words as vividly as Kelly did: still feeling her father's presence in small, unexpected moments — in the wind, in a song that catches her off guard on the radio, in quiet instances that have nothing overtly to do with him but somehow still do.

She was direct about how hard the year has been, calling it the most difficult thing she's ever had to go through. At the same time, she didn't frame her grief as something purely negative. She reflected on the depth of her love for her father and described the ability to have loved someone that completely as the greatest privilege of her life, even while acknowledging that the grief itself is now something she carries every single day rather than something that fades with time.

One of the more tender parts of Kelly's tribute involved her young son, Sidney. She wrote about noticing flashes of Ozzy in him — in his smile, in small mannerisms, in something intangible about his spirit — and said that resemblance has become a genuine source of comfort for her over the past year. It's a common thread in how families process the loss of a beloved parent or grandparent: finding pieces of the person who's gone reflected forward in the next generation, especially in children too young to have known them well.

Kelly's post also widened out from personal memory into a broader tribute to Ozzy's legacy and character. She spoke about his working-class roots in Birmingham, England, and how, despite becoming one of the most recognizable rock frontmen in history as the voice of Black Sabbath and later as a solo artist, he never lost touch with where he came from. That grounded quality is something bandmates, collaborators, and family members have described consistently over the decades, even as Ozzy's public persona veered into the theatrical and, at times, the genuinely chaotic.

She praised his honesty, his loyalty, his courage, and his humor as the traits that defined him most, and said that the year since his death has changed her in ways she never fully anticipated when it began. Grief, as Kelly described it in the post, isn't something you simply move through and come out the other side of unchanged — it reshapes you along the way, whether or not you're ready for that.

Kelly closed her tribute on a note that tied together both the public and private sides of who Ozzy Osbourne was. She acknowledged that his music will endure — Black Sabbath's influence on heavy metal is foundational and unlikely to fade — but she made clear that, for her family, what truly lasts isn't the catalog or the legend. It's the bond, the laughter, and the love they built with him directly, something she said death could never actually take away, no matter how much it's changed their day-to-day lives without him in it.

Ozzy Osbourne's death last year closed out one of the most improbable and enduring careers in rock history, one that took him from Birmingham's industrial working-class streets to global fame as the frontman of Black Sabbath, through a chaotic and often self-destructive solo career, and eventually into a kind of unlikely reality-television patriarch status via The Osbournes. Along the way, he became known as much for his resilience — surviving decades of substance abuse, health scares, and a very public battle with Parkinson's disease in his later years — as for his music itself.

A year on, it's clear from both Sharon and Kelly's tributes that the Osbourne family isn't interested in presenting a sanitized, purely triumphant version of Ozzy's memory. Instead, both women leaned into what made him real: the humor, the honesty, the imperfection, and the unmistakable presence that, even a year after his death, they say they still feel in the quiet, ordinary moments of everyday life.

title: "I'm Alive By Mistake": The Ryanair Passenger Who Was Sucked Out of a Plane Window Speaks Out
excerpt: Weeks after being violently pulled halfway out of a Ryanair window at 15,000 feet, Ljubiša Karović is opening up about a trauma that hasn't loosened its grip — and it's proving just as serious as his physical injuries.
body: Some survival stories don't fade with time — they just get harder to hear. That's exactly what's happening with Ljubiša Karović, the 61-year-old Serbian entrepreneur who, on July 10, was violently pulled halfway out of a Ryanair aircraft window at 15,000 feet. Weeks later, he's not just recovering physically — he's opening up about a trauma that, by his own account, hasn't loosened its grip at all.
What Actually Happened

Karović was flying with his wife, Svetlana, on Ryanair flight FR1879 — operated by Malta Air — from Thessaloniki, Greece, to Memmingen, Germany, headed to celebrate his brother's birthday. He had settled into window seat 11C when, moments after takeoff, he heard what he described as a sound like an explosion. The aircraft's window had shattered, and the sudden loss of cabin pressure created a force strong enough to pull him out of his seat and partway out of the plane.

His lawyer, Vasilis Tsiaras, later put the physics of the moment in stark terms: at a speed of more than 600 km/h, Karović ended up with his head and right arm outside the aircraft. He lost consciousness almost immediately as the cabin depressurized. Tsiaras didn't mince words describing the odds his client faced, calling him 'alive by mistake.'

What likely saved his life was the people around him. Svetlana, seated three rows behind him, ran forward and grabbed his legs to keep him from being pulled out entirely. She later described the moment with brutal honesty: she grabbed on thinking that if they were going to die, at least they'd die together. Other passengers, initially frozen in shock, quickly joined in — one man, believed to be Albanian, first tried using a bag to block the shattered window, which was immediately sucked out, before grabbing a suitcase that finally held. Passengers pulled Karović back inside together, his face visibly deformed from the trauma, blood pouring from his nose and mouth.

Ryanair confirmed that the flight returned to Thessaloniki shortly after takeoff following the mid-air incident. Preliminary findings, according to Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary, point to the possibility that the engine suffered foreign-object damage — essentially, that debris struck the engine, causing part of it to break off and strike the window next to Karović. The exact cause remains under formal investigation.
The Injuries — and the Invisible Ones

Karović's physical injuries were severe: damage to his head, eye, and ear, friction burns, injuries to his spine and shoulder, and temporary paralysis on one side of his body. Doctors have told him and his wife that his recovery will likely take months and could require multiple additional surgeries.

But in interviews since the incident, Karović has been just as candid about the psychological toll — arguably more so. He says he now suffers panic attacks whenever he hears the sound of an airplane. He's described himself as being 'at rock bottom' mentally, saying plainly that he is 'destroyed' and that the experience has fundamentally altered his life. He's said he can no longer go outside easily, that 'everything bothers' him, and that he has no intention of ever flying again.

Speaking to press, he's returned repeatedly to the sound — the explosion, the chaos — as the detail that won't leave him. It's the moment before everything that seems to replay the most, the noise that 'is always there' when he tries to sleep. That detail matters clinically too: it's a common feature of post-traumatic stress, where the mind fixates not on the outcome but on the instant everything changed.
A Story That's Still Unfolding

What makes this a genuine update story rather than a one-time news flash is that Karović's account has been deepening over several weeks, not fading. Early coverage focused on the mechanics of the incident and Ryanair's official statement. As the days passed, more human detail emerged — his wife's account of physically holding onto him, the stranger who helped seal the window, the surgeries still ahead, and now, most recently, the mental health toll that's proving just as serious as the physical injuries.

This pattern is worth noting for anyone following the story: the full picture of a traumatic incident rarely arrives all at once. The first 24 hours produce the facts — what happened, who was involved, what the airline says caused it. The weeks that follow produce the human cost — what the survivors are actually living with once the cameras and initial headlines move on. Karović's case is a clear example of that second, slower wave of reporting, and it's arguably the more important one for understanding what an incident like this really costs the people who survive it.
What This Means for Ryanair — and Air Travel Scrutiny

The incident adds to a run of uncomfortable headlines for Ryanair and for budget aviation more broadly. Questions about aircraft maintenance, engine integrity, and how airlines communicate with passengers during in-flight emergencies tend to resurface whenever an incident like this makes international news. Ryanair's own statement acknowledged that the window 'dislodged inflight' and that the aircraft made an emergency return — a fairly clinical description of an event that, for the people onboard, was anything but routine.

For now, the investigation into the exact cause remains open, and neither Ryanair nor aviation authorities have issued a final determination on what specifically caused the engine damage. Until that report lands, the story will likely keep circling back to two threads: what technically failed on that aircraft, and what it actually did to the people who were on it.
The Bigger Picture

Karović's case is a reminder that survival and recovery are not the same thing, and that 'he's alive' is often just the first sentence of a much longer story. His physical wounds have a rough timeline — months, more surgeries, an uncertain but plausible path to healing. His psychological wounds don't come with the same kind of roadmap. Panic at the sound of a plane engine isn't something that resolves on a surgical schedule, and there's no indication yet of what support, if any, he's receiving to work through it.

What's striking, reading his own words across multiple interviews, is the contrast between the language of luck — 'I am lucky,' 'alive by mistake' — and the language of devastation — 'destroyed,' 'rock bottom.' Both are true at once. He survived something that, by every account from people at the scene, he very plausibly shouldn't have. And surviving it hasn't made it easier to live with.

As the investigation into the mechanical cause continues, Karović's own account is likely to remain the more human, and more lasting, part of this story — not what broke on the plane, but what it broke in him.
Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to Ljubiša Karović on the Ryanair flight? He was partially sucked out of a shattered aircraft window at 15,000 feet after debris, believed to have come from the engine, struck and broke the window during a flight from Thessaloniki to Memmingen on July 10, 2026.

What injuries did Karović suffer? He sustained damage to his head, eye, and ear, friction burns, spinal and shoulder injuries, and temporary paralysis on one side of his body, along with ongoing psychological trauma including panic attacks.

What caused the window to break? Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary said preliminary findings suggest the engine may have suffered foreign-object damage, though the official cause remains under investigation.
Is Karović expected to recover? Doctors have said his physical recovery will take months and may require multiple additional surgeries. He has also spoken publicly about ongoing psychological trauma.

title: Kim Kardashian And Lewis Hamilton's Relationship Takes A Sweet New Turn With Adorable Puppy Addition
excerpt: Kim Kardashian and Lewis Hamilton's relationship just got a lot more official — meet Halo, the Formula 1 star's new golden retriever puppy.
body: Kim Kardashian and Lewis Hamilton's relationship has been the subject of speculation for months, but their latest joint venture might be the clearest sign yet that things between them are serious. The pair have welcomed a new furry addition into their lives — a golden retriever puppy named Halo — and Kardashian couldn't resist introducing her to the world.
Meet Halo

The seven-time Formula 1 world champion, 41, recently welcomed the new puppy, and it didn't take long for Kardashian, 45, to share the moment with her millions of followers. In a recent Instagram post captioned “lakemaxxing,” documenting snapshots from a lakeside getaway, Kardashian included a particularly sweet photo of herself cuddled up with Halo, instantly sending fans into a frenzy.

Halo's arrival was first confirmed publicly by Goldiva Goldens, a respected Maine-based golden retriever breeder. In a since-noted Instagram post, the breeder wrote, “We're excited to fly Ms Halo to Los Angeles to Formula 1 Ferrari driver @lewishamilton!!” The announcement came after months of speculation from fans, many of whom had been quietly hoping Hamilton would add a new dog to his family ever since he shared photos of himself surrounded by a litter of golden retriever puppies earlier in the year.

Halo made the journey from Maine to Los Angeles accompanied by dog trainer Kirstin McMillian, a third-generation animal trainer who had already travelled out to meet the puppy ahead of the move. Notably, McMillian is the same trainer who worked with Hamilton's two previous dogs, signalling just how much thought and continuity has gone into welcoming Halo into the family.
A New Chapter After Loss

Hamilton has long been known throughout the Formula 1 world for his deep love of dogs, and Halo's arrival marks an emotional new chapter following a difficult stretch for the racing star. His beloved English bulldog, Roscoe, became a fixture of the F1 paddock throughout Hamilton's years with Mercedes and was adored by fans across the sport. Roscoe sadly passed away in September 2025 at the age of 12, following a battle with pneumonia that Hamilton documented closely and openly with his followers at the time.

Roscoe wasn't Hamilton's only canine companion over the years. His other bulldog, Coco, had been by his side since 2013 but passed away in 2020 following a suspected heart attack at just six years old. Both dogs held a special place not just in Hamilton's personal life, but in the wider F1 community, regularly appearing alongside him at races and becoming beloved figures among supporters and fellow drivers alike.

Given that history, the arrival of Halo represents more than just a new pet — it's a meaningful step for Hamilton, nearly a year on from losing Roscoe, as he opens his life back up to a new four-legged companion. Fans and fellow F1 followers have responded warmly to the news, with many expressing genuine happiness that Hamilton has found room in his life for a new dog after such a significant loss.
Fans React To The New Arrival

Unsurprisingly, Halo's debut on social media sparked an outpouring of affection online. On Reddit, one fan summed up the general sentiment perfectly, writing, “This dog has no idea how lucky it is, gonna be spoiled rotten and probably have the best life a dog can have.”

Given Hamilton's track record with Roscoe and Coco — both of whom lived largely charmed, well-travelled lives alongside one of the most recognisable athletes in the world — it's safe to say that expectation is a fairly accurate one. Halo is reportedly from championship-winning bloodlines, with both of her parents having competed and won titles on the dog show circuit, suggesting she'll be in good company both on the family tree and in her new Los Angeles home.
What This Means For Kim And Lewis

Beyond the pure cuteness factor, Halo's arrival has added fresh fuel to the ongoing conversation about just how serious Kardashian and Hamilton's relationship has become. The pair have been linked since February, though multiple reports suggest they've actually been quietly seeing each other since as early as December.

Since going public, the couple has given fans plenty to speculate about, showing up together at a string of high-profile events and destinations across the globe. Throughout February and March, the pair were spotted on trips spanning Paris, the Super Bowl, and Arizona, before later appearing together in Tokyo and at Coachella in April. Each appearance added another layer to the growing narrative that this wasn't just a casual pairing, but something both parties were genuinely invested in.

Welcoming a pet together — even one that technically belongs to Hamilton — is often seen as a significant relationship milestone, and Kardashian's willingness to feature so prominently in Halo's introduction to the world suggests she's fully embracing her role in this new chapter of Hamilton's life. Whether or not the couple eventually gets a pet of their own together down the line, Halo's arrival has undeniably added a new layer of domesticity to a relationship that's been closely watched by fans and tabloids alike for months.
A Pattern Of Public Milestones

Kardashian and Hamilton's relationship has followed an interesting pattern since it first came to light — one defined by a steady drip of public appearances and shared moments rather than one single, dramatic reveal. From high-profile red carpet appearances to more low-key travel snapshots like the recent lakeside getaway, the couple has slowly built out a public narrative piece by piece, letting fans watch the relationship develop in near real-time.

Halo's introduction fits neatly into that pattern. Rather than a formal announcement, the puppy made her social media debut through candid, lifestyle-style photos — the kind that feel personal and unstaged rather than heavily managed for PR purposes. That approach has arguably made the relationship feel more genuine to fans who've followed its progression since the earliest rumours began circulating.
Hamilton's Long History With Dogs

For longtime F1 followers, Hamilton's love of dogs is far from a new development. Roscoe, in particular, became something of a paddock celebrity in his own right during Hamilton's dominant years with Mercedes, frequently photographed alongside trophies, team gear, and even wearing custom merchandise. His presence at races became such a fixture that his eventual passing was met with an outpouring of tributes not just from fans, but from figures across the sport.

That history adds extra weight to Halo's arrival. This isn't a driver picking up a pet on a whim — it's a continuation of a well-established, deeply personal part of Hamilton's life, now entering a new chapter with a new companion, a familiar trainer, and, notably, a high-profile partner along for the ride.
Final Thoughts

Whether you're following the story for the Formula 1 angle, the celebrity relationship angle, or simply because you can't resist a golden retriever puppy story, Halo's introduction to the world has managed to check every box. For Hamilton, it marks an emotional and hopeful new chapter following the loss of two beloved companions. For Kardashian, it's another small but telling glimpse into a relationship that continues to grow more serious with each public appearance.

As for Halo herself, with championship bloodlines, an experienced trainer, and two of the world's most recognisable public figures in her corner, it's safe to say she's settling into what fans are already calling an extremely spoiled — and extremely lucky — new life.

title: Love Island Winner Lorenzo Lands Surprise New Career Just Days After Leaving The Villa
excerpt: Fresh off his Love Island 2026 win with Julia, Lorenzo Alessi has already landed a surprising new gig — becoming Vogue's newest agony uncle. Here's everything we know.
body: Most Love Island winners spend the days after leaving the villa catching up on sleep, reuniting with friends and family, and slowly adjusting to life without cameras following their every move. Lorenzo Alessi, on the other hand, appears to be doing things a little differently.

Just days after being crowned this year's winner alongside partner Julia Majchrzak, the 28-year-old businessman has already landed a brand-new gig — and it's not the influencer deal or brand partnership most fans might have expected. Instead, Lorenzo has stepped into the world of relationship advice, becoming Vogue's newest agony uncle.
From The Villa To Vogue HQ

The move marks a genuinely unusual pivot for a reality TV winner. Rather than leaning purely into modelling deals or sponsored content, Lorenzo is now using the very thing that defined his time on the show — his relationship journey, complete with its ups, downs, and plenty of drama — to offer advice to real people navigating their own messy love lives.

In his first appearance for the publication, cameras captured Lorenzo sitting in Vogue's headquarters, working through a stack of reader-submitted dilemmas. The questions ranged from lighthearted to genuinely tricky, and Lorenzo appeared to lean directly into his own villa experience for guidance.

One reader had accidentally called their partner by an ex's name and asked how to recover from the slip-up. Lorenzo's advice was refreshingly direct: own the mistake, acknowledge there's no taking it back, and consider a grand gesture — flowers, coffee, some good old-fashioned grovelling — to smooth things over.

Another submission came from someone who had been accused of having an affair with their best friend and wanted to know how to convince their partner the relationship was strictly platonic. Drawing on lessons from his own experience navigating tangled connections in the villa, Lorenzo suggested getting everyone together for a drink in the same room, steering well clear of anything that could be read as sarcastic or dismissive, and letting the genuine friendship speak for itself.

Perhaps the most striking response came when a reader asked whether they should prioritise a promising new relationship or take a chance on appearing on a dating show themselves. Despite having just won the biggest dating show on British television, Lorenzo didn't hesitate to encourage them to choose the relationship instead, reportedly telling them that “lightning doesn't strike twice,” and that if you've found something good in real life, you should hold onto it for dear life given how tough dating can be otherwise.
Why Vogue, And Why Lorenzo?

The partnership is a notable one within the world of reality TV alumni. Only a small handful of former Love Island contestants have worked with Vogue in the past, including Maura Higgins, Molly-Mae Hague, and Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu — all of whom went on to build significant post-villa careers in fashion and media. Lorenzo joining that shortlist so soon after his win suggests the publication sees genuine crossover appeal in his personality and story.

It's not hard to see why. Lorenzo's season was defined by one of the more complicated and closely followed journeys of the entire series. He entered the villa with a self-described history of “situationships” and had never been in a serious, committed relationship before. That reputation, combined with his laid-back and self-deprecating sense of humour, quickly made him a fan favourite — even as some viewers and fellow islanders jokingly labelled him a potential “walking red flag” because of his casual approach to dating.

Throughout the series, Lorenzo navigated connections with several different islanders, including Julia, Yasmin, and Ellie, all while fielding accusations that he was more interested in the exposure and business opportunities the show could offer than in actually finding a genuine connection. He and Julia eventually solidified their relationship following the Casa Amor twist, becoming “exclusive” before the season's end — even though, notably, they were the only finalist couple who never explicitly told each other they were “in love.”

That messy, evolving journey is arguably exactly why Lorenzo's advice resonates. Rather than presenting himself as someone who had love figured out from day one, his season showcased real uncertainty, real mistakes, and real growth — all qualities that make his newfound role as an agony uncle feel a lot more authentic than it might coming from a contestant whose relationship played out picture-perfectly on screen.
A Historic Villa Win

Lorenzo and Julia's win wasn't just personally significant for the pair — it also made history for the show itself. After weeks of bombshell arrivals, explosive re-couplings, emotional Casa Amor reunions, and no shortage of villa drama, the pair beat out six fellow finalists to take the crown, splitting a £50,000 cash prize between them.

ITV later revealed the voting figures behind the win, with Lorenzo and Julia securing a commanding 62.4% of the public vote — nearly double their nearest competitors. It was a decisive victory that reflected just how invested viewers had become in their story throughout the series, despite — or perhaps because of — its rocky patches.

When asked by ITV how he planned to spend his share of the winnings, Lorenzo kept things relatively low-key, saying he wanted to treat himself to a meaningful memento of the experience, potentially a watch, as a way of commemorating the milestone.
Staying Grounded Since Leaving The Villa

Despite the whirlwind of new opportunities, both Lorenzo and Julia have kept a relatively low profile on their personal social media accounts since returning home, choosing not to flood their followers with immediate content the way some past winners have. That said, Lorenzo did give fans one particularly memorable glimpse into his post-villa life.

During his time on the show, Lorenzo became known for a very specific, very detailed description of his usual Saturday night routine — one that involved ironing his bedsheets to house music before heading out for the evening. “Every Saturday afternoon I iron my bedsheets,” he explained during the series, adding that “it gets you ready for the evening.” His routine continued with a night out, followed by a shower, and finally, a distinctly unglamorous nightcap: a bottle of water and exactly two Ferrero Rocher chocolates before bed.

Shortly after leaving the villa, Lorenzo shared a photo to his Instagram Stories that immediately confirmed he hadn't been exaggerating for the cameras — a snap of his freshly ironed bedsheets, complete with two Ferrero Rochers placed neatly on top. He offered no caption or explanation, but he didn't need one. Fans instantly recognised the reference and flooded the post with reactions, delighted that his quirky routine was very much a real, ongoing part of his life outside the villa.
What's Next For Lorenzo

Before entering the villa, Lorenzo's Instagram following sat somewhere in the modest range of one to four thousand followers. Since his season aired, that number has ballooned to nearly a quarter of a million, giving him a significantly larger platform to build on.

His background also includes some notable celebrity connections that surprised fans during the show's “Friends and Family” segment. Lorenzo's father, Oz, is a former high-profile celebrity bodyguard and works as a doorman at Sheesh, the celebrity-favoured restaurant based in Chigwell, Essex. Through his father's connections, Lorenzo has informal ties to a number of well-known names, including musician Zayn Malik, actor Danny Dyer, and former Love Island star Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu.

With a growing platform, a genuine and relatable personal story, and now a foothold in one of fashion's most recognisable publications, Lorenzo appears to be positioning himself for a media career that extends well beyond the usual reality TV shelf life. Whether the Vogue partnership becomes a recurring column or a one-off feature remains to be seen, but for now, it's clear his journey from the villa to relationship commentator is only just getting started.

title: Where Is The Clueless Cast Now? Everything We Know After Alicia Silverstone's Reboot Confirmation
excerpt: Alicia Silverstone is officially returning as Cher Horowitz in a new Clueless sequel series. Here's where the rest of the beloved 1995 cast is today.
body: Thirty-one years after “Clueless” first taught an entire generation how to properly use the word “whatever,” Cher Horowitz is officially coming back. Paramount+ has greenlit a sequel series to the 1995 cult classic, with Alicia Silverstone reprising her most iconic role and stepping into the executive producer's chair alongside original director Amy Heckerling.

The news has sent longtime fans of the film spiralling into a nostalgic rabbit hole, revisiting one of the most quotable, most stylish teen comedies of the '90s. But it's also raised an obvious question: what happened to the rest of that unforgettable cast, and will any of them be joining Silverstone in Beverly Hills for round two?
Here's a full breakdown of where everyone from the original “Clueless” ensemble stands today, and what we actually know about the upcoming series so far.
The Sequel Series: What We Know

The new Paramount+ series picks up 30 years after the events of the original film. According to the official synopsis, Cher Horowitz has, by most measures, figured her life out. She's a successful businesswoman who has mastered motherhood — until her teenage daughter starts high school and sends her right back into unfamiliar, “clueless” territory all over again.

It's a clever inversion of the original premise: instead of watching a privileged teenager navigate the chaos of Beverly Hills High, viewers will now watch her attempt to parent a teenager of her own, presumably while still delivering perfectly timed one-liners in equally perfect outfits.

The project wasn't always destined for Paramount+. A “Clueless” revival had previously been in development at Peacock, with Silverstone attached from the start, but that version of the series was quietly dropped by the streamer in early 2026. It never advanced to production and never aired in any form. Paramount+ has now stepped in, given the concept a fresh start, and reportedly ordered six episodes, with filming expected to begin in Los Angeles in 2027.

The series will be written by Josh Schwartz and Stephanie Savage — the duo behind “Gossip Girl” — alongside Jordan Weiss, known for creating “Dollface” and co-writing “Freakier Friday.” Silverstone and Heckerling will both executive produce, alongside producer Robert Lawrence and several others through CBS Studios, keeping much of the creative DNA of the original film intact.

As for the rest of the cast, nothing has been officially confirmed. Paul Rudd, Stacey Dash, Donald Faison, and other “Clueless” alumni have not been attached to the new series, and outlets covering the announcement have noted there's currently no word on their potential involvement. Any returning castmates would presumably be announced as the project moves closer to production in 2027.
Alicia Silverstone (Cher Horowitz)

Silverstone was just 18 years old when “Clueless” launched her into the spotlight, and the role has followed her — in the best possible way — for the rest of her career. Before Cher, she'd already appeared in a handful of films, but it was her turn as the impeccably dressed, endlessly well-meaning Beverly Hills teen that made her a household name.

Since then, Silverstone has built a genuinely varied filmography, including “Batman & Robin” in 1997, “Vamps” in 2012, and Yorgos Lanthimos's unsettling “The Killing of a Sacred Deer” in 2017. More recently, she's appeared in “Reptile” (2023), “Pretty Thing” (2025), and the Oscar-nominated “Bugonia.”

Away from acting, Silverstone has become known almost as much for her activism as her filmography. She's a committed animal and environmental-rights advocate and founded The Kind Life, a platform dedicated to sharing plant-based living and eco-conscious lifestyle content. She's also stayed connected to her “Clueless” roots over the years, reprising Cher briefly for a 2023 Super Bowl commercial for Rakuten alongside her former on-screen rival, Elisa Donovan.
Elisa Donovan (Amber Mariens)

No discussion of “Clueless” is complete without Amber, Cher's snobbish, endlessly entertaining high school rival. Elisa Donovan brought the character to life with a perfect blend of vanity and comic timing, and Amber's rivalry with Cher remains one of the film's most quoted dynamics.

Donovan has continued acting steadily since the film, and like Silverstone, she reprised her role for the same 2023 Rakuten Super Bowl ad, proving the on-screen chemistry between Cher and Amber is still very much intact decades later. Fans have been hopeful that Donovan could make an appearance in the new series, even if only in a cameo capacity.
Donald Faison (Murray Duvall)

Donald Faison, who played Dionne's on-again, off-again boyfriend Murray, went on to have one of the most successful post-“Clueless” careers in the original cast. His breakout came with a starring role as Dr. Chris Turk on “Scrubs,” a part he played for nine seasons and later reprised in the show's 2026 ABC reboot.

Faison has spoken fondly about the idea of a “Clueless” reunion in the past. In a February 2024 interview with PEOPLE, he expressed enthusiasm about the concept of a sequel centered on the original characters' kids, joking that Cher would essentially become the new Mel Horowitz — her father's character from the original film. He also speculated that Cher and her on-screen love interest Josh would likely still be together decades later, even if it might feel “a little weird” to imagine.
The Rest Of The Ensemble

While Silverstone, Donovan, and Faison have remained the most visible members of the cast in recent years, the film's ensemble included several other now-iconic performances — Paul Rudd as Josh, Breckin Meyer as Travis, Jeremy Sisto as Elton, and Stacey Dash as Dionne, among others. None of these actors have been officially confirmed for the new series at this stage, though speculation is running high given how beloved the original cast remains.

One name that will inevitably come up in any “Clueless” retrospective is Brittany Murphy, who played the endearing Tai Frasier. Murphy tragically passed away in 2009, and she will not be part of the new series' returning ensemble. Fans on social media have already expressed hope that the show will find a thoughtful way to honour her memory and contribution to the film's legacy.
Why This Reboot Feels Different

2026 has been something of a banner year for nostalgic television revivals. Netflix has announced a reboot of “A Different World,” the beloved spin-off of “The Cosby Show,” while a “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” revival — which even had original star Sarah Michelle Gellar attached — was ultimately cancelled by Hulu before making it to air.

Given how mixed the results of legacy reboots have been in recent years, there's understandable skepticism whenever a beloved property gets the sequel treatment. Plenty of these revivals have amounted to little more than brand maintenance, trading on nostalgia without adding anything meaningful to the original story.

But there's reason to believe the “Clueless” sequel could be different. Unlike many revivals that bring back a project with none of the original creative team involved, this series has Silverstone, Heckerling, and Lawrence all actively shaping the direction of the new story. That level of creative continuity is relatively rare and suggests a genuine effort to honour what made the original film work, rather than simply cashing in on the name recognition.

Paramount+'s head of original programming, Jane Wiseman, echoed this sentiment in a statement, calling the project a “homecoming” for the franchise and emphasizing the studio's commitment to filming in Los Angeles — the city that helped make the original film such a defining piece of '90s pop culture.
What Fans Can Expect Next

With filming not expected to begin until 2027, there's still a long runway before fans get their first real look at the new series. In the meantime, speculation about casting, plot details, and potential cameos from the original ensemble is likely to dominate conversation among longtime fans of the film.

One thing seems certain: three decades on, “Clueless” remains one of the most beloved and quotable teen comedies ever made, and its influence on fashion, pop culture, and the high-school comedy genre as a whole is still being felt today. Whether the new series can capture that same lightning-in-a-bottle magic remains to be seen, but with Silverstone and Heckerling both back at the helm, expectations are cautiously — and enthusiastically — high.

title: What Actually Happens To Your Body In The 24 Hours After You Die, According To A Former Death Investigator
excerpt: A retired NYC death investigator with 23 years of field experience explains, hour by hour, what happens to the human body in the first day after death — from rigor mortis to bacterial breakdown.
body: Death is one of the few universal experiences no one gets to talk about afterward, which is exactly why so many people are quietly fascinated by what actually happens once the heart stops. For most of us, the subject stays firmly in the “too morbid to ask about” category. But for Barbara Butcher, it was a full-time job for more than two decades — and she's finally pulling back the curtain on what really goes on inside a body in the first 24 hours after death.

Butcher spent 23 years working as a death investigator for the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, a role that put her at some of the most harrowing scenes imaginable, including the recovery and identification efforts following the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center. If anyone has earned the right to talk candidly about death, it's her.

In a recent sit-down interview posted on YouTube, Butcher walked viewers through exactly what happens to human remains in the hours immediately following death — and the details are as scientifically fascinating as they are unsettling.
Why The First 24 Hours Matter So Much

For a death investigator, the first day after someone dies isn't just biologically significant — it's professionally critical. The changes a body goes through in this window are one of the main tools investigators use to estimate time of death, which can be the difference between solving a case and hitting a dead end (pun very much intended).

Butcher explained that her job largely revolved around reading the body like a clock. Every stage of physical change, from stiffening muscles to shifting blood, tells a story about how long ago someone passed away. It's a skill built on pattern recognition, science, and — as she describes it — a lot of hands-on experience with things most people will never see in their lifetime.
Stage One: Rigor Mortis Sets In

The most well-known post-death change is rigor mortis, the temporary stiffening of the body's muscles. Contrary to what most people assume, rigor mortis doesn't hit the entire body all at once. It's a gradual process that starts small and spreads.

According to Butcher, the stiffening typically begins in the smaller muscle groups first — the jaw, the neck, and the fingers — before eventually working its way into the larger muscles of the body. This progression isn't random. It follows a fairly predictable pattern that experienced investigators can use to their advantage.

“It happens over time. It's a progression,” Butcher explained, noting that a body will typically reach full rigor within eight to ten hours after death. From there, the body generally stays in that fully stiffened state for roughly another twelve hours before gradually beginning to soften again as the chemical processes driving the stiffness start to break down.

This means that within the first 24 hours, a body can move through almost the entire rigor mortis cycle — from flexible, to rigid, to starting the process of relaxing once more. For someone trained to notice it, the specific muscle groups affected and the degree of stiffness present can help narrow down a fairly precise window for when death occurred.

Butcher noted that she could often tell whether a body was heading into rigor or coming out of it based on which muscles were affected and to what degree — a skill that became second nature after years in the field, but one that takes serious training and exposure to develop.
Why Rigor Mortis Happens At All

For those wondering about the science behind it, rigor mortis is caused by chemical changes at a cellular level. When a person is alive, muscle cells constantly use a molecule called ATP to allow muscle fibres to contract and relax. Once death occurs, the body stops producing ATP, and without it, the proteins responsible for muscle movement — actin and myosin — essentially get locked in place. This is what creates that characteristic stiffness.

Eventually, as the body's cells begin to break down through natural decomposition, those chemical bonds deteriorate, and the rigidity fades. That's why rigor mortis is temporary rather than permanent, even though it can feel like a strange and unsettling process to imagine.
Stage Two: Bacteria Takes Over

While rigor mortis is happening on the outside, something equally significant is happening on the inside — and according to Butcher, it happens fast. Within the first 24 hours, bacteria in the body essentially runs wild.

While a person is alive, the immune system keeps the trillions of bacteria that naturally live in and on the human body in check. The moment death occurs, that regulation disappears. With no immune system left to hold them back, bacteria — particularly the kind that live in the gut — begin multiplying rapidly and spreading through the body's tissues.

This bacterial activity is one of the earliest drivers of decomposition. It's also part of the reason bodies begin to change colour, develop odours, and undergo other visible transformations relatively quickly after death, particularly in warmer environments.
Location, Temperature, And Season All Matter

One point Butcher was keen to stress is that there's no single, universal timeline for what happens after death. The specifics — how fast rigor mortis sets in, how quickly bacterial decomposition becomes visible, how the body's appearance changes — depend heavily on environmental conditions.

Where a person is located when they die, the ambient temperature, and even the time of year can all speed up or slow down these processes significantly. A body in a hot, humid climate will decompose far more quickly than one in a cold, dry environment. This is actually one of the fundamental principles used in forensic science: investigators don't just look at the body in isolation, they look at the body in the context of its surroundings.

This is also why forensic pathologists and investigators often work with a range of clues — body temperature, lividity (the pooling of blood due to gravity), the degree of rigor, insect activity, and environmental data — rather than relying on any single indicator to establish time of death. Butcher's expertise lay in reading all of these signs together to build the most accurate picture possible.
Who Is Barbara Butcher?

Butcher isn't just a talking head sharing internet-friendly trivia — she's one of the most respected names in American forensic investigation. During her 23-year tenure at the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, she became known for her calm, methodical approach to some of the city's most difficult cases.

Her most high-profile and emotionally taxing work came in the aftermath of September 11, 2001, when she was part of the team responsible for the painstaking task of recovering and identifying victims of the World Trade Center attacks. It's the kind of work that requires not just scientific expertise but an extraordinary amount of emotional resilience.

Since retiring, Butcher has become something of a public educator on the realities of death and forensic science, sharing her decades of firsthand experience through interviews, books, and now video content aimed at demystifying a subject most people avoid.
Why This Kind Of Content Resonates With So Many People

There's a reason content like this consistently performs well online — true crime, forensic science, and death-related education have become some of the most engaged-with genres across YouTube, podcasts, and social media over the last several years. Shows built entirely around forensic pathology, real-life death investigators, and true crime breakdowns have amassed enormous, loyal audiences.

Part of the appeal is simple curiosity. Death is something every person will eventually experience, yet it remains one of the least discussed topics in everyday life. Hearing directly from someone who spent decades working with the dead offers a rare, grounded perspective — free from horror-movie exaggeration and instead rooted in real biology and lived professional experience.

There's also an educational angle. Understanding what happens to the body after death can be genuinely useful information, whether it's satisfying general curiosity, helping someone process grief, or simply making an uncomfortable topic feel a little less mysterious and a little more human.
The Bigger Picture: What This Teaches Us About Forensic Science

Butcher's breakdown of the first 24 hours after death is also a useful window into how forensic science actually works in practice, as opposed to how it's often dramatized on television. Real investigative work isn't about flashy technology solving a case in minutes — it's about patient, methodical observation of biological processes that unfold in predictable, science-backed stages.

The progression of rigor mortis, the spread of bacterial activity, and the influence of environmental factors are all pieces of a much larger puzzle that trained professionals use to answer one of the most important questions in any death investigation: when did this person die?

For investigators like Butcher, that question isn't just academic. Establishing an accurate time of death can be crucial for identifying victims, corroborating or disproving witness accounts, and ultimately helping bring closure to grieving families or, in some cases, helping bring perpetrators to justice.
Final Thoughts

It's not every day you get a first-hand, expert breakdown of exactly what happens to the human body after death, delivered by someone who spent over two decades doing the work in one of the busiest medical examiner's offices in the world. Barbara Butcher's insight into rigor mortis, bacterial breakdown, and the many variables that affect decomposition offers a rare, honest look at a subject most people spend their whole lives avoiding.

Whether you're drawn to it out of scientific curiosity, a fascination with true crime, or simply a desire to understand more about the natural world, Butcher's decades of frontline experience make for one of the more compelling — and educational — deep dives into what really happens after we die.
